title: Their analogy: Scripture stands to the Church as a dogma stands to Scripture
source_text: XXV. Verum ut distinctius appareat discrimen Pontificiae sententiae, et nostrae, et qua in re positus sit controversiae cardo, sciendum est Pontificios ita Scripturam sacram cum Ecclesiae doctrina comparare, ut nos aliquod fidei particulare dogma cum Scriptura sacra comparamus. Sicut ergo aliquem fidei articulum, ut exemp. gr. mortuos olim resurrecturos esse, in se suam veritatem et authoritatem a solo Deo habet, non vero a testimonio Prophetarum et Apostolorum, qui Scripturae libros conscripserunt: ita Pontificii admittunt Scripturam sacram in se suam authoritatem a solo Deo habere, non ab Ecclesiae testimonio. Deinde quemadmodum praecipua ratio fidei, qua dogma illud amplectimur non est proprie Petri, Pauli, Esaiae, etc. authoritas, sed divina revelatio ad nos illorum calamo transmissa, quandoquidem ante Scripturam dogma illud creditum fuit, et adhuc citra Scripturam credi potest. Sic fatentur Pontificii, Ecclesiae testimonium non esse fidei nostrae de Scriptura rationem propriam atque praecipuam, sed simpliciter et absolute divinam revelationem. Rursus tamen, ut dogma illud, et aliud quodvis simile non debet publice in Ecclesia recipi, et credendum proponi, nisi quatenus Scripturae testimoniis probatur ex quibus solis publice constare potest fidelibus aliquid ad fidem pertinere, atque sic dogmatis cujusvis authoritas quoad nos, et certitudo publica et externa a Scripturae sacrae testimonio pendet: Ita volunt Pontificii Scripturae authoritatem quoad nos ab Ecclesiae testimonio pendere, neque de libri alicujus divinitate publice fidelibus constare, nisi ex Ecclesiae approbatione et testificatione. Denique, quemadmodum, non obstante illa dogmatum a Scriptura dependentia, religionis Christianae dogmata multis, praeter Scripturae testimonia, argumentis probari et suaderi possunt, quae tamen argumenta non sunt fidei nostrae ratio et fundamentum, sed tantum motiva quaedam ad fidem inducentia: Ita Pontificii quoque non diffitentur Scripturam sacram, praeter Ecclesiae testimonium, multa divinitatis argumenta et notas habere, quibus probari et suaderi possit, sed quae tamen non possunt publicam de Scripturae divinitate fidem in Ecclesia fundare.
pass_a_gloss: But so that the difference between the Pontifical sentence and ours may appear more distinctly, and where the hinge of the controversy is placed, it must be known that the Pontificii compare sacred Scripture with the Church's doctrine as we compare some particular dogma of faith with sacred Scripture. Just as therefore some article of faith — for example that the dead will one day rise — has in itself its truth and authority from God alone, and not from the testimony of the Prophets and Apostles who wrote the books of Scripture: so the Pontificii admit that sacred Scripture has in itself its authority from God alone, not from the Church's testimony. Next, just as the chief reason of faith by which we embrace that dogma is not properly the authority of Peter, Paul, Isaiah, and so on, but the divine revelation transmitted to us by their pen — since that dogma was believed before Scripture, and can still be believed apart from Scripture — so the Pontificii confess that the Church's testimony is not the proper and chief reason of our faith concerning Scripture, but simply and absolutely divine revelation. Yet again, just as that dogma, and any other like it, ought not to be publicly received in the Church and proposed for belief except insofar as it is proved by Scripture's testimonies, from which alone it can be publicly established for believers that something belongs to faith, and so any dogma's authority with respect to us, and its public and external certainty, hangs on sacred Scripture's testimony: so the Pontificii want Scripture's authority with respect to us to hang on the Church's testimony, and the divinity of any book not to be publicly established for believers except from the Church's approval and attestation. Finally, just as — that dependence of dogmas on Scripture notwithstanding — the dogmas of the Christian religion can be proved and urged by many arguments besides Scripture's testimonies, which arguments yet are not the reason and foundation of our faith but only certain motives leading to faith: so the Pontificii also do not deny that sacred Scripture, besides the Church's testimony, has many arguments and notes of divinity by which it can be proved and urged, yet which cannot found public faith concerning Scripture's divinity in the Church.
pass_b_english: To mark the difference between their sentence and ours, and where the hinge of the controversy sits, note how the Pontificii compare sacred Scripture with the Church's doctrine: as we compare a particular dogma of faith with sacred Scripture.

As an article of faith — for example that the dead will one day rise — has its truth and authority in itself from God alone, not from the Prophets' and Apostles' testimony as writers of Scripture, so they admit that sacred Scripture has its authority in itself from God alone, not from the Church's word.

And as the chief reason we embrace that dogma is not properly Peter's, Paul's, or Isaiah's authority, but the divine revelation brought to us by their pen — for the dogma was believed before Scripture, and can still be believed apart from it — so they confess that the Church's testimony is not the proper and chief reason of our faith about Scripture, but simply and absolutely divine revelation.

Yet again: as that dogma, or any like it, must not be publicly received in the Church or set forth for belief unless Scripture's testimonies prove it — since only from those can believers publicly know that something belongs to faith, so that any dogma's authority for us, and its public external certainty, hangs on sacred Scripture's testimony — so they want Scripture's authority for us to hang on the Church's testimony, and a book's divinity not to be publicly settled for believers except by the Church's approval and attestation.

Finally: even with that dependence of dogmas on Scripture, Christian dogmas can be proved and urged by many arguments besides Scripture's testimonies — motives that lead toward faith, not faith's reason and foundation. So the Pontificii also do not deny that sacred Scripture, besides the Church's testimony, has many notes and arguments of divinity by which it can be proved and urged — yet which cannot found public faith in the Church concerning Scripture's divinity.
